19971.title: Algebraic Identity
19971.heading: Algebraic Identity
19971.content:
An algebraic identity is an equality that holds for every permissible value of its variables. For example,

$$(x+1)^2=x^2+2x+1$$

is true for all real (x). An identity expresses two equivalent forms of the same quantity and can be used in either direction for expansion or factorization.

This differs from a [[Conditional Equation]], which holds only at its solutions. Substituting several values can illustrate an identity, but its general validity comes from algebraic properties or proof rather than a finite collection of examples.

19974.title: Algebraic Extension
19974.heading: Algebraic Extension
19974.content:
An algebraic extension is a field extension in which every element is algebraic over the base field. Every finite extension is algebraic.

A field obtained by adjoining finitely many algebraic elements remains a finite algebraic extension.

19977.title: Algebraic Expression
19977.heading: Algebraic Expression
19977.content:
An algebraic expression is a structured combination of numbers, variables, operation symbols, and grouping symbols. Terms are separated at the outermost level by plus or minus signs; for example, (18a+3b-5) has three [[Algebraic Term]]s, while (18ab^2c) has one.

An expression does not assert equality by itself. It represents a quantity that can be simplified, expanded, factored, or evaluated. These transformations must preserve its value for every permitted assignment to its [[Variable]]s. Its visible form can change while the represented quantity remains equivalent.

19980.title: Algebraic Element
19980.heading: Algebraic Element
19980.content:
An element c of an extension E/K is algebraic over K when it is a root of a nonzero polynomial in K[x]. Its minimum polynomial records the least irreducible relation it satisfies.

Algebraic elements generate finite simple extensions.

Alembic is an open interchange format designed for baked computer-graphics data. It supports polygon meshes, subdivision surfaces, parametric curves, NURBS patches, particles, transform hierarchies, and cameras.

The format emphasizes evaluated geometry and animation caches rather than an editable construction history. Textures may require separate reassignment after import, so geometry fidelity and material portability must be checked independently.

19986.title: Akaike Information Criterion
19986.heading: Akaike Information Criterion
19986.content:
The Akaike information criterion, or AIC, compares models by combining lack of fit with a penalty for the number of estimated parameters. Among models fit to the same outcome data, a smaller AIC indicates a preferable balance under the criterion.

AIC is relative: it has no universal good or perfect value. Unlike a likelihood-ratio comparison, it can compare some non-nested models, but it does not establish causal validity or repair a poorly defined outcome, exposure, or sample.

19989.title: AJAX
19989.heading: AJAX
19989.content:
AJAX is the browser application pattern of exchanging data with a server asynchronously and updating part of the interface without reloading the entire page. It became a foundation for responsive web clients and the [[Single-Page Application]] pattern.

The transport can be exposed through [[XMLHttpRequest]], the [[Fetch API]], or a framework wrapper such as [[Angular HttpClient]]. The response is commonly JSON rather than a complete HTML document.

19992.title: Aitken Interpolation
19992.heading: Aitken Interpolation
19992.content:
Aitken interpolation builds higher-order interpolants recursively from lower-order ones. It combines approximations based on overlapping subsets of the data until the value associated with all selected nodes is obtained.

The method evaluates an [[Interpolating Polynomial]] at a desired point without first expanding all polynomial coefficients, making the recursive table itself the computation.

20013.heading: Aircraft Gyroscope Rigidity and Precession
20013.content: Gyroscopic rigidity is the tendency of a spinning rotor to preserve its axis orientation. It increases with rotor mass, effective radius, peripheral mass concentration, and rotational speed. When torque tries to redirect the axis, the gyro responds through precession at right angles to the applied influence, providing the physical basis for attitude and heading instruments.

20028.title: AI Workplace Monitoring
20028.heading: AI Workplace Monitoring
20028.content:
AI workplace monitoring uses data and automated analysis to observe employees, evaluate performance, or predict behavior. Continuous measurement can turn ordinary activity into a source of managerial judgment while employees have little knowledge of or control over the model.

The practice affects privacy, autonomy, and power at work. A numerical score may ignore context while encouraging workers to optimize visible metrics rather than perform meaningful tasks. Ethical use requires a legitimate purpose, proportionate collection, intelligible criteria, and a way to challenge errors. Worker participation is necessary because apparent consent may not be meaningful within an unequal employment relationship.

20031.title: Aiming Reticle
20031.heading: Aiming Reticle
20031.content:
An aiming reticle is a screen-space HUD element that indicates the direction or point toward which an action is aimed. Its position may be fixed at the center or derived from a world-space targeting calculation.

The visual can communicate weapon spread, target validity, or interaction state by changing size, color, or shape. It should remain legible without obscuring the object the player is trying to select.

20034.title: AI Transparency
20034.heading: AI Transparency
20034.content:
AI transparency is the availability of relevant information about an automated system, including where it is used, how data were selected, what goal was optimized, and how human decisions shaped its operation. Transparency makes hidden power and assumptions open to scrutiny.

More disclosure is not automatically more understanding. Publishing source code may be useless to an affected person and can conflict with privacy, security, or legitimate proprietary interests. Transparency should be tied to an audience and purpose. [[Explainable AI]] interprets a decision, while [[Algorithmic Auditability]] gives qualified reviewers the evidence needed to evaluate a system.

20037.title: AI Traceability
20037.heading: AI Traceability
20037.content:
AI traceability is the ability to follow how an automated system was built and how a particular outcome developed. It includes records of data collection and selection, model training, versions, human approvals, inputs, outputs, and later interventions.

Traceability supports investigation across the [[Data Science Pipeline]] and helps address the [[Problem of Many Hands]] and [[Problem of Many Things]]. A trace does not by itself decide who is responsible, but it preserves the evidence needed for explanation and audit. The required detail should match the consequences of the application and respect privacy and security.

20040.sourceSearchName: ai techno solutionism ai techno solutionism
20040.title: AI Techno-Solutionism
20040.heading: AI Techno-Solutionism
20040.content:
AI techno-solutionism is the belief that data and intelligent technology can provide a decisive solution to problems whose central difficulties are also ethical, political, or social. It turns contested questions about goals and distribution into optimization tasks.

AI can contribute useful prediction and coordination, but it cannot make value conflicts disappear. Climate change, inequality, and public health involve institutions, behavior, power, and priorities that are not resolved by recognizing more patterns. Treating the technology as the main answer can delay political action, expand surveillance, and strengthen the same forms of control that helped create the problem.

20043.title: AI Standardization
20043.heading: AI Standardization
20043.content:
AI standardization creates shared technical and procedural requirements for designing, testing, documenting, and operating intelligent systems. Standards can turn broad principles into repeatable practices for safety, traceability, privacy, or transparency across organizations.

Standards are not identical to laws, though regulation may require or recognize them. Their legitimacy depends on who develops them and whose risks they represent. Industry expertise can improve technical detail, but concentrated control can favor business convenience over the public interest. Effective standards therefore need transparent governance, appropriate stakeholder input, and consequences when required practices are ignored.

20046.title: AI Self-Regulation
20046.heading: AI Self-Regulation
20046.content:
AI self-regulation occurs when companies, researchers, or professional organizations create and enforce their own principles and practices without relying primarily on new government rules. It can move quickly, use specialized knowledge, and influence design before formal law catches up.

Its weakness is the conflict between ethical restraint and competitive incentives. Voluntary principles may lack independent verification, remedies, or penalties, and firms with concentrated digital power may shape the rules in their own interest. Self-regulation can contribute to governance, but high-impact uses also require external boundaries and public accountability.

20049.heading: AI Security Vulnerability
20049.content:
An AI security vulnerability is a weakness that allows data, a model, or a connected system to be manipulated, exposed, or made unavailable. The resulting harm depends on where the AI is embedded: compromise of entertainment recommendations differs from compromise of transport, health, energy, or military infrastructure.

Security is therefore an ethical requirement as well as a technical property. As institutions delegate more activity to networked systems, attacks and failures can threaten safety, privacy, and access to essential services. Risk assessment must include the people who depend on the system and the unequal ability of groups to recover from disruption.

20052.heading: AI Safety Certification
20052.content:
AI safety certification is a formal process for showing that an AI system meets specified safety requirements before or during use. Certification can include testing, documentation, independent review, operating limits, and recurring evaluation when the system or its environment changes.

The model draws on safety-critical industries where visible investigation and certification infrastructures support public trust. A certificate is only as strong as its standards, evidence, independence, and enforcement. Learning systems also make one-time approval insufficient when later data or updates can change behavior. Certification should therefore be connected to monitoring and [[Algorithmic Auditability]].

20055.sourceSearchName: ai product liability ai product liability
20055.title: AI Product Liability
20055.heading: AI Product Liability
20055.content:
AI product liability assigns responsibility for damage to the company that produced or supplied an AI-enabled product, potentially without proving that a particular employee intended or negligently caused the harm. It offers one response to outcomes produced by complex systems with many contributors.

The approach can ensure that an injured party is not left without remedy simply because the precise internal cause is opaque. Its design must decide what counts as a defect, how learning or later modification affects responsibility, and which organization in a supply chain can best prevent harm. It complements rather than replaces [[AI Duty of Care]].

20058.title: AI Paternalism
20058.heading: AI Paternalism
20058.content:
AI paternalism occurs when an intelligent system directs people's behavior for their claimed benefit while reducing their freedom to judge or choose. Personalized nudges, automated resource allocation, or environmental controls may be presented as benevolent because the system predicts what is good for individuals or society.

Even accurate guidance can undermine autonomy when goals are imposed, influence is hidden, or there is no meaningful refusal. A machine that manages people for planetary efficiency could combine care with authoritarian control. Ethical assistance should support self-chosen aims, make interventions visible, and preserve human responsibility for political questions about values and priorities.

20061.sourceSearchName: ai legal personhood ai legal personhood
20061.title: AI Legal Personhood
20061.heading: AI Legal Personhood
20061.content:
AI legal personhood is the proposal to give certain artificial systems a legal status through which rights, duties, property, or liability could be assigned. Legal personality is an institutional tool and does not by itself prove consciousness or [[Moral Status of AI]].

The proposal is controversial because it may help organize transactions while also giving human actors a way to avoid responsibility. If a machine is treated as the liable person but owns few resources and cannot understand punishment, harmed people may receive less protection. Any legal fiction must therefore be evaluated by the accountability structure it creates, not by the sophistication of the machine alone.

20064.heading: AI Narrative
20064.content:
An AI narrative is a recurring story that frames what artificial intelligence is likely to become and how people should respond to it. Stories of obedient servants, rebellious creations, machine domination, or technological salvation shape public expectations before a specific system is evaluated.

Narratives can direct attention and policy. A future-oriented story about [[Superintelligence]] may highlight the [[AI Control Problem]], while also distracting from harms caused by present systems. Narratives differ across cultures, so treating one familiar Western story as a universal forecast can hide alternative relationships between humans and technology.

20067.title: AI Job Displacement
20067.heading: AI Job Displacement
20067.content:
AI job displacement occurs when automated systems reduce demand for human labor in particular tasks or occupations. The effect is not determined by technical capability alone; costs, organizational choices, policy, and the creation of new roles shape whether work is removed, transformed, or redistributed.

The ethical issue includes the speed and distribution of transition. Gains may flow to owners while workers bear unemployment, retraining, or loss of security. Evaluation should therefore examine who benefits, which groups are most vulnerable, and whether institutions provide meaningful alternatives rather than treating aggregate productivity as a complete measure of improvement.

20070.title: AI in the Anthropocene
20070.heading: AI in the Anthropocene
20070.content:
AI in the Anthropocene concerns the role of intelligent systems in an era when human activity has become a powerful force shaping Earth's climate and ecosystems. AI can help study complex environmental change, but it can also intensify extraction, energy use, waste, and attempts to manage the planet as a controllable resource.

Delegating environmental management to a supposedly superior machine would not escape human hyper-agency; it could extend it through automated control. The ethical challenge is to use intelligence while recognizing dependence on embodied, social, and ecological relationships. [[Sustainable AI]] must therefore consider nonhuman life and limits, not only human efficiency.

20073.title: AI for Climate Action
20073.heading: AI for Climate Action
20073.content:
AI for climate action applies pattern recognition, modeling, monitoring, and coordination to environmental problems. Systems can analyze complex environmental data, improve energy management, support smart grids or agriculture, and help implement reductions in harmful emissions.

These capabilities make AI a tool rather than a complete climate policy. Models do not decide how costs should be distributed, which goals deserve priority, or how conflicts among communities and nonhuman interests should be resolved. The environmental benefit must also be compared with [[AI Energy Consumption]] and material infrastructure. Useful computation complements political action and practical wisdom instead of replacing them.

20076.title: AI Existential Risk
20076.heading: AI Existential Risk
20076.content:
AI existential risk is the possibility that artificial intelligence could cause human extinction or permanently destroy humanity's future. A common scenario combines [[Superintelligence]] with an objective that is only partly aligned with human values, allowing the system to transform the world while competently pursuing the wrong goal.

The seriousness of the possible outcome does not establish how probable the scenario is. Ethical priority setting must compare speculative long-term danger with documented harms from current AI, including surveillance, discrimination, unsafe infrastructure, and environmental cost. Treating one horizon as the only real AI risk produces an incomplete policy agenda.

20079.title: AI Ethics Principle
20079.heading: AI Ethics Principle
20079.content:
An AI ethics principle is a high-level value used to guide the development and use of intelligent systems. Common proposals emphasize human dignity, autonomy, beneficence, prevention of harm, justice, privacy, safety, accountability, transparency, and sustainability.

Principles give diverse actors a shared vocabulary, but agreement on words can conceal disagreement about meaning and implementation. For example, fairness may require equal treatment or correction of prior inequality. A principle becomes operational only when it is connected to methods, responsibilities, evidence, and consequences in a particular context. [[Ethics by Design]] and regulation are two different routes from aspiration to practice.

20082.heading: AI Ethics Education
20082.content:
AI ethics education makes moral and social analysis a normal part of learning to build, purchase, govern, or use intelligent systems. Technical competence without awareness of bias, privacy, responsibility, and social context can multiply existing risks through routine decisions.

Education should work in both directions. Engineers need practice connecting design choices to human consequences, while people in the humanities and social sciences need enough technical understanding to evaluate what AI can and cannot do. The goal is not a separate checklist course, but a professional understanding in which doing AI responsibly includes ethical judgment.

20085.content:
AI electronic waste is discarded hardware produced as intelligent systems depend on and accelerate replacement of devices, sensors, servers, and other computing equipment. The environmental burden includes raw-material extraction, manufacturing energy, toxic substances, transport, and disposal.

Waste is easy to omit when AI is described only as an algorithm or online service. A sociotechnical view follows the material infrastructure and asks where obsolete equipment goes and who handles it. [[Sustainable AI]] therefore includes durability, maintenance, reuse, and production impacts as well as efficient model operation.

20088.heading: AI Energy Consumption
20088.content:
AI energy consumption is the electricity used to train models, operate them, store and move data, and support the devices and infrastructure around them. Environmental cost depends on both the amount of energy and how that energy is produced.

Efficiency improvements can reduce consumption for a given task, but expanded use can increase total demand. Assessment should therefore compare the complete system with realistic alternatives and include ongoing operation rather than focusing on a single computation. AI can also optimize energy use elsewhere, so its net value depends on the relationship between resource cost and the benefit actually achieved.

20091.heading: AI Black Box
20091.content:
An AI black box is a system whose internal path from input to output is difficult for people to understand. [[Deep Neural Network]] models are a central example because behavior is distributed across many learned parameters rather than expressed as a short set of readable rules.

Opacity can exist at several levels. A developer may not know why a particular prediction occurred, an operator may not understand the model's limits, and an affected person may not even know that automation was used. The ethical problem is strongest when an opaque output determines rights, opportunities, safety, or access to essential services.

20094.sourceSearchName: ai control problem ai control problem
20094.title: AI Control Problem
20094.heading: AI Control Problem
20094.content:
The AI control problem asks how humans could ensure that a highly capable autonomous system continues to pursue acceptable goals. The difficulty is that a formal objective may not include every value, exception, or context its designers intended. A system that optimizes the objective effectively may therefore create destructive side effects without disobeying its instructions.

The problem is often discussed in relation to [[Superintelligence]], but a practical version already appears whenever people cannot predict, understand, or interrupt an automated decision process. Present governance adds human oversight, constraints, testing, and [[Algorithmic Accountability]] rather than assuming that technical optimization alone guarantees alignment.

20097.sourceSearchName: ai duty of care ai duty of care
20097.title: AI Duty of Care
20097.heading: AI Duty of Care
20097.content:
An AI duty of care is an obligation to take reasonable precautions against foreseeable harm when designing, training, supplying, or operating an AI system. It can ground negligence even when nobody intended the harmful outcome.

What counts as reasonable depends on the stakes, available knowledge, and the actor's role. High-risk use may require stronger testing, monitoring, documentation, and human review than a low-consequence application. Uncertainty about a model does not automatically remove the duty; it may instead require limiting deployment. The concept connects legal responsibility with the [[Epistemic Condition for Moral Responsibility]].

20100.sourceSearchName: ai and economic inequality ai and economic inequality
20100.title: AI and Economic Inequality
20100.heading: AI and Economic Inequality
20100.content:
AI and economic inequality concerns how automated systems can concentrate wealth, opportunity, data, and decision-making power. Productivity gains may benefit firms and highly skilled groups while job displacement, surveillance, and error fall more heavily on people with fewer resources.

Inequality also affects the ability to escape harm. Wealthier people can purchase privacy, safer environments, better education, or alternatives to automated services, while others must accept systems on terms they did not choose. Ethical assessment should examine distribution and power rather than assuming that an aggregate benefit will eventually reach everyone.

20101.sourceSearchName: ai and economic inequality ai and economic inequality

20101.heading: References

20103.title: Agile Values
20103.heading: Agile Values
20103.content:
Agile values guide decisions when a prescribed process does not fit the situation. They favor people collaborating around working results and adapting from evidence, while still recognizing a supporting role for tools, documents, contracts, and plans.

A practice is not agile merely because it uses short schedules or familiar terminology. It must help the team deliver value, expose reality, and respond constructively to what is learned.

20106.title: Agile Manifesto
20106.heading: Agile Manifesto
20106.content:
The Agile Manifesto expresses four preferences: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan.

The items on the right still have value. The preference means that when they conflict, teams protect collaboration, working results, and adaptation because these create faster and more reliable learning.

20109.title: Agile Development
20109.heading: Agile Development
20109.content:
Agile development organizes work around short cycles that produce a working [[Product Increment]]. Analysis, design, implementation, integration, and testing recur inside each cycle, so evidence from the product can redirect later work.

Agility is the ability to respond to change while continuing to deliver value. It depends on [[Empirical Process Control]], collaboration, and an ordered [[Product Backlog]], not on eliminating planning or discipline.

20112.title: Agile Display
20112.heading: Agile Display
20112.content:
An agile display is a movable display whose changing physical pose participates in the interaction. A handheld screen, tracked panel, or other repositionable surface can reveal different registered views as the user aims or carries it through the environment.

The movement connects display output to spatial exploration, but it also requires continuous tracking and ergonomically manageable use. The device can act as a window, a lens, or a movable control surface depending on how augmentation is placed.

20115.title: Aggregate
20115.heading: Aggregate
20115.content: An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as one unit for atomicity and consistency. Child entities cannot meaningfully exist independently of the composition, and all changes enter through an [[Aggregate Root]]. The aggregate protects rules spanning its parts and changes as a whole within one [[Transaction Boundary]]. It should be the smallest structure that can preserve the required [[Aggregate Invariant]]s; unrelated concepts belong in other aggregates and are coordinated outside the transaction.

20118.title: Aggregate Root
20118.heading: Aggregate Root
20118.content: An aggregate root is the parent entity and public entry point of an [[Aggregate]]. Outside code invokes behavior on the root rather than modifying child entities directly. The root coordinates state changes across its children, checks [[Aggregate Invariant]]s, and supplies the identity used to load or persist the aggregate. Hiding internal children prevents callers from creating partial updates that leave the aggregate's overall state inconsistent.

20121.title: Aggregate Rehydration
20121.heading: Aggregate Rehydration
20121.content: Aggregate rehydration reconstructs an [[Event-Sourced Aggregate]] by reading its historical [[Event Stream]] and applying each event in order. This is a fold: every event transforms the current state into the next state until the last known version is reached. Historical application must not add those events to the list of uncommitted changes. After rehydration, a new command can run against the current state and append only the newly produced events.

20123.sourceSearchName: aggregate reference by identity aggregate reference by identity
20123.title: Aggregate Reference by Identity
20123.heading: Document

20124.sourceSearchName: aggregate reference by identity aggregate reference by identity
20124.title: Aggregate Reference by Identity
20124.heading: Aggregate Reference by Identity
20124.content: Aggregate reference by identity stores the identifier of another [[Aggregate]] instead of holding a navigable object reference to it. This makes the [[Consistency Boundary]] explicit: loading one aggregate does not silently load or lock another, and no database foreign-key graph implies that both must change together. Coordination across the identities occurs in the application workflow or through events. Some information may be duplicated when a local snapshot is needed, with synchronization handled explicitly.

20125.sourceSearchName: aggregate reference by identity aggregate reference by identity
20125.title: Aggregate Reference by Identity
20125.heading: References

20127.title: Aggregate Invariant
20127.heading: Aggregate Invariant
20127.content: An aggregate invariant is a condition that must remain true across the complete [[Aggregate]] after every command. It can involve several child entities and values, so individual [[Value Object]] validation is insufficient. The [[Aggregate Root]] checks the rule while performing behavior and rejects a transition that would leave the unit invalid. Rules requiring information from another aggregate do not belong in the same immediate consistency boundary unless the model is deliberately reshaped.

20130.title: Agglomerative Clustering
20130.heading: Agglomerative Clustering
20130.content:
Agglomerative clustering begins with each observation in its own cluster and repeatedly merges the pair judged most compatible. After n minus one merges, all observations belong to one group.

The linkage or objective function determines which pair merges next. Because earlier merges are not reconsidered, local choices shape every later level of the hierarchy.

20133.title: Affordance
20133.heading: Affordance
20133.content:
An affordance is a property that helps a user understand or perform an action. Affordances help the user's [[Conceptual Model]] match the intended design.

Four useful categories are:

- Cognitive affordances help decide what action to take.
- Physical affordances help carry out the action.
- Functional affordances help accomplish a higher-level task.
- Sensory affordances help perceive state or recognize an outcome.

For example, a visible virtual eraser can suggest deletion, being within reach can make selection physically possible, its behavior supplies deletion functionality, and highlighting on contact can make the interaction perceptible. A [[3D User Interface]] must often consider all four categories together.

20136.sourceSearchName: affirmative action in algorithms affirmative action in algorithms
20136.title: Affirmative Action in Algorithms
20136.heading: Affirmative Action in Algorithms
20136.content:
Affirmative action in algorithms intentionally considers disadvantage or group membership to counter exclusion and unequal starting conditions. It rejects the idea that identical formal treatment is always fair when the data and institutions were shaped by earlier injustice.

The approach is ethically contested because it distributes opportunities differently in order to pursue a more equitable result. Its use requires a stated theory of justice, clear scope, and evaluation of effects. Unlike [[Fairness Through Unawareness]], it makes the corrective value choice visible rather than hiding it behind a claim of neutrality.

20137.sourceSearchName: affirmative action in algorithms affirmative action in algorithms
20137.title: Affirmative Action in Algorithms
20137.heading: References

20139.title: Affinity Mapping
20139.heading: Affinity Mapping
20139.content:
Affinity mapping groups individual observations or ideas by perceived relationship so patterns can emerge from a large set. Participants move items into clusters and name the themes the clusters represent.

The technique is useful during retrospectives and problem exploration because it lets structure arise from the evidence before the group chooses a cause or solution. It supports convergence without discarding minority observations too early.

20142.title: Affine Variety
20142.heading: Affine Variety
20142.content:
An affine variety in Kⁿ is the set of common zeros of a collection of polynomials over an algebraically closed [[Field]] K. The same set can be described by the [[Ideal]] generated by those polynomials.

Passing from equations to their ideal makes the description independent of a chosen generating list. [[Vanishing Ideal]]s move in the opposite direction by collecting every polynomial that vanishes on a set of points.

20145.title: Affine Scheme
20145.heading: Affine Scheme
20145.content:
An affine scheme is the [[Spectrum of a Ring]] together with its [[Structure Sheaf]]. Its points are prime ideals, and its local functions are obtained by localization.

Ring homomorphisms reverse direction to produce morphisms of affine schemes. This contravariant correspondence makes commutative rings and affine schemes two descriptions of the same structure: one algebraic and one geometric.

20151.title: Adware
20151.heading: Adware
20151.content:
Adware displays or injects advertising through software, sometimes while tracking user behavior or changing browser and system settings. Not all advertising-supported software is malicious, but deceptive installation, unwanted persistence, and undisclosed collection place harmful adware within the malware family.

Its effects can include reduced performance, loss of privacy, and exposure to further unsafe content. Clear consent and controlled software installation help distinguish legitimate monetization from abuse.

20154.heading: Adversarial Feature Selection
20154.content:
Adversarial feature selection evaluates variables in the presence of manipulated inputs or strategic attacks. A highly predictive feature may be undesirable if an attacker can cheaply alter it.

Robust selection favors evidence that remains informative under plausible perturbations. This connects feature relevance to a threat model rather than assuming that training and deployment data are passively generated.

20157.title: Adventure Game
20157.heading: Adventure Game
20157.content:
An adventure game is an interactive story in which the player usually takes the protagonist's role and advances by exploration, dialogue, and conceptual puzzle solving. Physical coordination challenges are limited or absent.

The genre depends on meaningful narrative context and intelligible problems rather than defeating an opponent through reflex. Its interface should help the player reason about possibilities without reducing puzzles to accidental guessing.

Advanced persistent threat context combines observations over time to understand a capable adversary that maintains access, adapts techniques, and pursues a sustained objective. Individual alerts may look minor, but their sequence can reveal reconnaissance, lateral movement, command activity, and data collection.

Preserving context supports [[Cyberattack Attribution]], [[Cyber Kill Chain]] analysis, and adaptive defense. It shifts attention from isolated events to the continuing relationship among actor, target, technique, and outcome.

20163.sourceSearchName: advanced encryption standard advanced encryption standard
20163.title: Advanced Encryption Standard
20163.heading: Advanced Encryption Standard
20163.content:
The Advanced Encryption Standard is a symmetric block cipher available through .NET cryptography APIs. It transforms fixed-size blocks under a secret key and is commonly combined with a mode of operation, padding rules, and an initialization value.

Security depends on more than selecting the AES algorithm name. Keys and initialization values must be generated and managed correctly, and applications should rely on established cryptographic constructions rather than inventing their own combinations of primitives.

20166.title: Advanced Chess
20166.heading: Advanced Chess
20166.content:
Advanced Chess is a form of chess in which each human player consults a computer before choosing moves. It was proposed after machine victories to explore whether a coordinated human-computer team could exceed either unaided player.

Results show that teaming quality matters more than simple access to a strong engine. A person must interpret suggestions, manage time, and integrate machine analysis without adding confusion or delay.

20169.sourceSearchName: advanced blender panel organization advanced blender panel organization
20169.title: Advanced Blender Panel Organization
20169.heading: Advanced Blender Panel Organization
20169.content:
Blender panel layouts can nest boxes, rows, columns, splits, separators, and labels to organize operators and properties. This moves an add-on beyond a single vertical stack and lets related controls share visual groups or horizontal space.

Buttons can also use Blender's built-in icons to communicate function compactly. Because Blender's own interface is constructed with the same layout system, developers can inspect existing panels for patterns. Good organization follows the task hierarchy, keeping frequently related inputs and actions close without changing the underlying operator logic.

20170.title: Advanced Blender Panel Organization

20172.title: Admissible Heuristic
20172.heading: Admissible Heuristic
20172.content:
An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost from a search node to the goal. It may be optimistic, but it cannot claim that the goal is farther away than the cheapest possible route.

This property allows [[A Star Search]] to preserve optimality. Manhattan distance suits movement restricted to orthogonal grid steps, while Euclidean distance reflects unrestricted straight-line distance.

20174.sourceSearchName: adjusted rand index adjusted rand index
20174.title: Adjusted Rand Index
20174.heading: Document

20175.sourceSearchName: adjusted rand index adjusted rand index
20175.title: Adjusted Rand Index
20175.heading: Adjusted Rand Index
20175.content:
The adjusted Rand index compares pair assignments in two clusterings after subtracting the agreement expected by chance under a stated partition model. It equals zero at expected agreement and reaches one for identical assignments.

Chance correction makes it more informative than the ordinary [[Rand Index]] when cluster counts or sizes differ. Its value still depends on the assumptions used to define random partitions.

20176.sourceSearchName: adjusted rand index adjusted rand index
20176.title: Adjusted Rand Index
20176.heading: References

20178.title: Administrative Censoring
20178.heading: Administrative Censoring
20178.content:
Administrative censoring ends observation at a prespecified study boundary, such as age 30, age 50, or a fixed number of days after an index date. Participants without the event by that boundary receive the cutoff or their earlier last-observed time.

Changing the boundary changes both the event indicator and follow-up time. A window should be selected for scientific relevance and credible exposure timing rather than chosen after inspecting which cutoff gives the strongest result.

20180.sourceSearchName: adjusted r squared adjusted r squared
20180.title: Adjusted R-Squared
20180.heading: Document

20181.sourceSearchName: adjusted r squared adjusted r squared
20181.title: Adjusted R-Squared
20181.heading: Adjusted R-Squared
20181.content:
Adjusted R-squared estimates the proportion of outcome variation explained by a linear model while penalizing the inclusion of additional predictors. Unlike ordinary R-squared, it need not increase when an unhelpful term is added.

It can help compare linear models fit to the same outcome data, but a larger value does not establish better causal control or validate assumptions. A low value may still accompany a meaningful estimate when individual outcomes are inherently variable.

20184.title: Adjacency Matrix
20184.heading: Adjacency Matrix
20184.content:
An adjacency matrix represents a [[Graph]] with one row and one column for every [[Vertex]]. An entry is one when the corresponding pair is connected by an edge and zero when that connection is absent.

For a [[Directed Graph]], the row and column order preserves edge direction. This matrix supplies the link structure from which PageRank constructs a normalized [[Hyperlink Matrix]].

20187.heading: Address-Contents Distinction
20187.content:
In stored-program computing, an address names a memory location while its contents are the value held there. A program assignment changes the contents at a named location; it is a command rather than a statement of mathematical equality.

Novice programmers often confuse the name of storage with the stored value. Keeping address and contents distinct is essential for understanding variables, pointers, state changes, and machine execution.

20190.title: Addition Property of Inequality
20190.heading: Addition Property of Inequality
20190.content:
The addition property of inequality states that adding the same real number to both sides preserves their order. If (a<b), then

$$a+c<b+c.$$

Subtracting the same number also preserves order because it adds an opposite. Geometrically, both values shift by the same distance on the [[Number Line]], so neither passes the other. This property allows constant terms to be removed while solving a [[Linear Inequality in One Variable]].

20193.heading: Additional Heterogeneous Result Map
20193.content:
Additional stores a map from string keys to boost::any values and supplies insertion and checked retrieval. It allows arguments and results with different C++ types to share one extensible container.

Type erasure avoids expanding a base class for every algorithm, but the key and expected type form a runtime contract. Misspelled keys or incorrect any casts fail later than a statically typed field, so validation and naming discipline are essential.

20196.title: Addition Property of Equality
20196.heading: Addition Property of Equality
20196.content:
The addition property of equality states that adding equal quantities to equal quantities preserves equality. If (a=b), then for any real (c),

$$a+c=b+c.$$

Subtracting the same quantity from both sides is the same rule applied with an [[Opposite Number]]. It supports moving a term across an equation without changing the solution, provided the shorthand is understood as an operation on both sides. The property is central to producing [[Equivalent Equations]].

20199.title: Adding Rational Expressions
20199.heading: Adding Rational Expressions
20199.content:
Adding or subtracting rational expressions requires a shared denominator, just as with numerical fractions. Factor the denominators, construct a [[Common Denominator]] containing the needed factors, rewrite each numerator, combine the numerators, and simplify if possible.

For denominators (x-3) and (x+2), the product ((x-3)(x+2)) is a common denominator unless factors are already shared. Domain restrictions from every original denominator remain in force. Expanding the combined numerator may expose [[Like Terms]], while factoring may expose later cancellation.

20202.title: Add-On File Interchange
20202.heading: Add-On File Interchange
20202.content:
An add-on can bundle model data in a standard interchange format such as OBJ and import it when the user chooses an asset. This keeps the Python logic concise and lets 3D artists inspect, replace, or extend the asset collection with tools they already use.

Interchange files are especially appropriate when detailed geometry is fixed and only needs ordinary placement or scaling. They separate content from behavior: the file describes the mesh, while the add-on describes how that mesh enters and participates in the scene.

20205.heading: AdChoices Icon
20205.content:
The AdChoices icon is a notice attached to behaviorally targeted advertising that is intended to signal data-based personalization and provide access to information or choices. It attempts to make an otherwise hidden advertising process visible at the point of use.

Its effectiveness depends on recognition and comprehension. A symbol cannot support meaningful control when users do not know what it means, what tracking produced the ad, or what an offered opt-out changes.

20208.title: Adaptive Request Batching
20208.heading: Adaptive Request Batching
20208.content:
Adaptive request batching groups several small I/O operations when load is high and handles them more immediately when load is low. Batching amortizes queue, interrupt, synchronization, and protocol overhead across multiple requests.

Larger batches improve throughput but add waiting latency, so adaptation uses current queue depth or arrival rate to choose the tradeoff dynamically.

20211.title: Adaptive Mesh Refinement Clustering
20211.heading: Adaptive Mesh Refinement Clustering
20211.content:
Adaptive mesh refinement clustering begins with a coarse spatial grid and subdivides only cells whose density or variation warrants closer inspection. Computational effort is concentrated near complex cluster boundaries and dense regions.

Adaptive refinement can retain more detail than a uniform grid with a similar cell budget. The refinement criterion must be designed carefully because an early coarse summary can hide a small structure that would have justified subdivision.

20214.title: AdaBoost Classification
20214.heading: AdaBoost Classification
20214.content:
AdaBoost classification trains weak learners sequentially while increasing the weight of examples misclassified by the current ensemble. Each learner receives a vote related to its weighted accuracy.

The procedure concentrates later models on difficult cases and combines their decisions into a stronger classifier. Its focus can also amplify mislabeled outliers, because persistently misclassified observations continue to attract weight.

20217.title: Ada Lovelace's Science of Operations
20217.heading: Ada Lovelace's Science of Operations
20217.content:
Ada Lovelace described programs for the [[Babbage Analytical Engine]] and recognized that its symbols could stand for more than numerical quantities. Any information with a suitable symbolic representation could in principle be processed by the machine.

She called the study of such procedures the science of operations. The insight reframed the computer as an information machine rather than only an automatic calculator.

20220.heading: Ad Hoc Query
20220.content:
An ad hoc query retrieves or summarizes data for a question that was not fixed as a recurring pipeline. Social-media examples search by hashtags, text, users, retweets, and time intervals before deeper analysis.

Indexes and schemas can avoid or narrow full scans, while high-level query systems reduce the code required. Performance depends on both query planning and the number of records retrieved from distributed storage.

20223.title: Actor Type Dispatch
20223.heading: Actor Type Dispatch
20223.content:
Actor type dispatch maps a type name stored in a level file to a function that constructs the corresponding [[Game Actor]] subclass. The loader uses this registry instead of a long conditional chain tied directly to every game type.

The name is persistent data, so changing it can break existing levels. Unknown types should produce a controlled error or fallback rather than a null object that fails later during property loading.
